story: The Federal Aviation Administration's draft environmental assessment of Zipline International's request to fly commercial drone package delivery over five Texas metro areas, Amarillo, Austin, El Paso, Houston and San Antonio, open for public comment until October 11th, 2026. Record item tx-2026-0186.
resourced: WebFetch returned HTTP 403 Forbidden on 2026-09-24 for both https://www.faa.gov/uas/advanced_operations/nepa_and_drones and the draft EA PDF. Every quote below was therefore checked character for character against the showrunner's same-day curl copies at /home/user/TexasAIDocket/out/2026-09-24/tmp/faa_nepa.txt and /home/user/TexasAIDocket/out/2026-09-24/tmp/zipline_ea.txt, and not against a live fetch of mine. zipline_ea.txt is NOT whitespace-collapsed as described. It keeps the PDF's line breaks, so a quote that crosses a line break is matched with each break read as one space. The line numbers in each claim's location field are zipline_ea.txt line numbers.
notes: The fact-checker had no shell tool this run, so it could not execute claims_check.py --template or --file. The schema was taken from the source of /home/user/TexasAIDocket/scripts/carousel/claims_check.py. REQUIRED is id, text, quote, url, source_type and retrieved. SOURCE_TYPES is primary_official, primary_corporate, secondary_reported and data. The gate requires no story block and no source_title. Both appear here as extra fields. The showrunner must run claims_check --file on this file.

Every EA claim is primary_official, because it is a NEPA filing the FAA published for comment. Its own text says Zipline prepared it under FAA supervision (c6). So every capability claim is written as what the draft describes, never as an established fact about the aircraft. It is a draft. No decision, FONSI or OpSpecs amendment exists in either source.

c26, c27 and c28 were not scout candidates. They were found and verified by the fact-checker during the sweep, and they are marked origin fact_checker. c26 is the story's own noise premise. The showrunner may drop any of them.

claims.text: Zipline International is seeking Federal Aviation Administration approval to begin commercial package delivery operations in five Texas metro areas. They are Amarillo, Austin, El Paso, Houston and San Antonio.
claims.quote: Zipline International Inc. (Zipline) is seeking FAA approval to begin commercial package delivery operations in five Texas metropolitan areas: Amarillo, Austin, El Paso, Houston, and San Antonio.
claims.source_title: FAA, Public Involvement and Environmental Review for Drone Operations
claims.location: Environmental Documents for Public Review, Zipline Texas entry

claims.text: Comments on the draft environmental assessment are due to the FAA by October 11th.
claims.quote: Please review the Draft EA and submit your comments by October 11, 2026.
claims.source_title: FAA, Public Involvement and Environmental Review for Drone Operations

claims.text: The FAA takes comments by email at 9-FAA-Drone-Environmental@faa.gov and asks that the subject line name the Zipline Texas Draft EA.
claims.quote: Comments should be submitted to: 9-FAA-Drone-Environmental@faa.gov . Please reference the Zipline Texas Draft EA in the email subject line when sending comments.
claims.source_title: FAA, Public Involvement and Environmental Review for Drone Operations
claims.note: The space before the period after the address is in the source. The EA's own notice (zipline_ea.txt lines 28 to 33) also accepts written comments by U.S. mail to FAA, Suite 802W, C/O AVS Environmental, 800 Independence Avenue, Washington, DC 20591.

claims.text: The FAA notice says the draft became available for a 30-day public review beginning on Friday, September 11th.
claims.quote: The Draft EA will be available for a 30-day public review beginning on Friday, September 11, 2026.
claims.source_title: Draft Environmental Assessment for Zipline International Inc. Proposed Drone Package Delivery Operations in Multiple Texas Metropolitan Areas, September 2026
claims.location: FAA Notice of Availability, lines 25 to 26

claims.text: The FAA notice says every substantive comment received will be responded to in the final environmental assessment.
claims.quote: All substantive comments received will be responded to in the final EA.
claims.source_title: Draft Environmental Assessment for Zipline International Inc. Proposed Drone Package Delivery Operations in Multiple Texas Metropolitan Areas, September 2026

claims.text: The draft states that Zipline, the applicant, prepared it under FAA supervision.
claims.quote: Zipline prepared this draft environmental assessment (draft EA) under the supervision of the FAA
claims.source_title: Draft Environmental Assessment for Zipline International Inc. Proposed Drone Package Delivery Operations in Multiple Texas Metropolitan Areas, September 2026
claims.note: In the source the word after 'the' is 'FAA7', with a footnote 7 marker citing 42 U.S.C. 4336a(f) and FAA Order 1050.1G. The quote stops before the marker. Every preparer listed in Appendix C (lines 2419 to 2430) is at ICF, and the Appendix D noise report reads 'PREPARED FOR: Federal Aviation Administration' and 'PREPARED BY: ICF'. Copy should keep the document's own wording, 'Zipline prepared', and must not imply that Zipline staff wrote every page.

claims.text: The draft's totals row caps the proposal at 220 Chargers, 4,400 Dropboxes, 220,000 maximum deliveries per day and 660,000 maximum transits per day. Houston and San Antonio are each allotted up to 65 Chargers, 1,300 Dropboxes and 65,000 deliveries per day.
claims.source_title: Draft Environmental Assessment for Zipline International Inc. Proposed Drone Package Delivery Operations in Multiple Texas Metropolitan Areas, September 2026
claims.note: A flattened table. The column order comes from header lines 318 to 331: Area (square miles), Zipline Chargers, Zipline Dropboxes, Maximum Deliveries per Day, Maximum Transits per Day. The same rows appear in Table 1 of the Appendix E letter (lines 4345 to 4350). The text uses only figures the table prints. Nothing was summed.

claims.text: The draft counts three transits in every delivery. A drone flies from a Charger to a Dropbox, then from the Dropbox to the delivery location, then from the delivery location to a Charger.
claims.quote: Each delivery includes three transits: 1) flight from Charger to Dropbox, 2) flight from Dropbox to delivery location, and 3) flight from delivery location to ending Charger.
claims.source_title: Draft Environmental Assessment for Zipline International Inc. Proposed Drone Package Delivery Operations in Multiple Texas Metropolitan Areas, September 2026
claims.location: Appendix E, FAA Section 7 letter to USFWS, footnote a to Table 1, lines 4351 to 4352
claims.note: THE DOCUMENT CONTRADICTS ITSELF HERE. The same footnote under Table 2.2-1 in the body (lines 338 to 339) gives leg 3 as '3) flight from Dropbox to ending Charger.' This claim uses the Appendix E wording because it agrees with the body at lines 356 to 358: a drone would 'undock from a Charger, fly to a Dropbox to pick up a package, make a delivery, and return to a Charger'. Confidence is medium only because the two versions disagree. See rejected.

claims.quote: Approximately 95% of flights would take place during 7:00 am to 10:00 pm and 5% of flights would take place during 10:00 pm to 7:00 am.
claims.source_title: Draft Environmental Assessment for Zipline International Inc. Proposed Drone Package Delivery Operations in Multiple Texas Metropolitan Areas, September 2026

claims.source_title: Draft Environmental Assessment for Zipline International Inc. Proposed Drone Package Delivery Operations in Multiple Texas Metropolitan Areas, September 2026

claims.text: The aircraft has a wingspan of approximately 7.8 feet, a height of approximately 1.8 feet and a length of approximately 8 feet.

claims.text: The draft says Zipline drones automatically deconflict with each other through a combination of strategic and tactical avoidance measures.
claims.quote: Zipline UAs automatically deconflict with each other using a combination of strategic and tactical avoidance measures
claims.source_title: Draft Environmental Assessment for Zipline International Inc. Proposed Drone Package Delivery Operations in Multiple Texas Metropolitan Areas, September 2026
claims.location: Section 2.2.4, lines 471 to 473. The sentence is repeated in section 3.7.2, lines 2052 to 2054
claims.note: The scout's quote stopped mid-phrase at 'strategic and'. It was extended by the next two words, 'tactical avoidance measures', so that it ends on a complete noun phrase. The extension is still verbatim.

claims.text: At a delivery the pod is lowered on a winch line and steers its own lateral position while it evaluates the delivery location. It descends the rest of the way only if the location is clear.
claims.quote: The pod is released from the Zipline UA and lowered to the ground via the winch line. During pod descent, the pod automatically controls its position laterally and evaluates the delivery location. If the delivery location is clear, the pod would continue to descend and deliver the payload at the delivery target.

claims.location: Section 2.2.4.6 Delivery, lines 563 to 567. Repeated in the Appendix E letter, lines 4518 to 4521
claims.note: The winch line runs from a hover at 330 feet AGL (line 563 and c11). This section describes the delivery without any operator step. See c18.

claims.text: When the pod can't automatically identify the delivery target and evaluate its suitability, the draft says an image is sent to an operator for real-time evaluation.
claims.quote: If the pod is unable to automatically identify the delivery target and evaluate its suitability, an image is sent to an operator for real-time evaluation.

claims.location: Section 3.7.2 Visual Effects, Affected Environment, lines 2070 to 2072
claims.note: This sentence appears ONLY in the visual effects section and not in the flight operations description in 2.2.4.6. The next sentence reads 'If the delivery site does not meet Zipline's evaluation criteria,22 delivery would not continue, and the pod is retracted back into the Zipline UA.' Footnote 22 (lines 2099 to 2100): 'Zipline's evaluation criteria includes visual clearance for obstacles. It may also include additional checks such as pod position tracking errors.' The document never says 'only'. See rejected.

claims.text: The noise report's delivery sequence has the aircraft hold a hover at 330 feet AGL while the pod is winched to the ground and stowed again, for approximately 75 seconds.
claims.quote: Maintain hover at 330 feet AGL as Droid is un-stowed from the P2 Zip, Droid is winched down to the ground at the delivery point, and Droid is re-stowed once delivery is complete (approximately 75 seconds).

claims.text: The draft applies the FAA Order 1050.1G test. Under it a noise impact is significant if the action raises DNL by 1.5 dB or more at a noise sensitive area exposed at or above DNL 65 dB, or brings an area to 65 dB or above through an increase of DNL 1.5 dB or greater.
claims.quote: FAA Order 1050.1G, Appendix A, states noise impacts would be significant if the action would increase the DNL by 1.5 dB or more for a noise sensitive area that is exposed to noise at or above DNL 65 dB, or that will be exposed to DNL values at or above 65 dB due to an increase of DNL 1.5 dB or greater, when compared to the no action alternative for the same timeframe.
claims.source_title: Draft Environmental Assessment for Zipline International Inc. Proposed Drone Package Delivery Operations in Multiple Texas Metropolitan Areas, September 2026

rejected.finding: Candidate 8 in the wording under Table 2.2-1 at page 2-2: 'Each delivery includes three transits: 1) flight from Charger to Dropbox, 2) flight from Dropbox to delivery location, and 3) flight from Dropbox to ending Charger.'
rejected.reason: The quote is verbatim at lines 338 to 339 and it is internally inconsistent. Its leg 3 goes from the Dropbox back to a Charger, which leaves out the return from the delivery point. The same footnote in the FAA's Appendix E letter to USFWS (lines 4351 to 4352) reads 'flight from delivery location to ending Charger'. That version agrees with the body at lines 356 to 358, 'fly to a Dropbox to pick up a package, make a delivery, and return to a Charger'. The Appendix E wording is carried as c8. The disagreement is a fact about the document that the record may report. It must not be resolved silently in copy.

rejected.finding: Candidate 23, the Appendix D Table 1 row 'Delivery hover for 75 s with package at MTOW Hover at 330 feet AGL UA in port orientation relative to the microphone, 50 feet away from delivery point 74.1'
rejected.reason: The string is verbatim at lines 2803 to 2808, but the figure doesn't mean what the row label says. In Table 9 of the same report (lines 3490 to 3501), 74.1 is the average of the as-tested port-side hovers at 50 feet. The report says hover tests ran 30 seconds and were time-corrected to 75 seconds (lines 3407 to 3410 and footnote lines 3504 to 3507). It gives a maximum adjusted SEL of 79.5 dBA at 50 feet, and Table 13 gives a delivery cycle of 79.9 dBA SEL at 50 feet. Publishing 74.1 as the sound of a 75 second hover would misstate the report's own analysis. SEL is also a single-event metric and can't be compared with the DNL 65 dB threshold in c20.

rejected.finding: The brief's framing that an operator is sent an image 'only when' the pod can't identify the target
rejected.reason: The document says 'If the pod is unable to automatically identify the delivery target and evaluate its suitability, an image is sent to an operator for real-time evaluation' (c18). It never says 'only', and it gives no rate or share of deliveries that reach an operator. The sentence appears in section 3.7.2 Visual Effects alone. The flight operations description in 2.2.4.6 and the Appendix E and F letters describe the delivery with no operator step. Copy may say what c17 and c18 say. It may not say 'only', 'rarely' or any frequency.

rejected.finding: Any count of the counties in the Section 106 letter, including the letter's own '41 counties'
rejected.reason: The letter says 'the entirety or portions of 41 counties in Texas' (line 7394). A tally of the names in the listed sentence (c25) made while reading came to 40. That tally is a model's count and is itself unverified, so neither number is cleared for publication. If a count is wanted, code must count the names in the c25 quote. The discrepancy with 41 should be reported as a discrepancy, never repaired.

rejected.finding: A live re-fetch of either source by the fact-checker
rejected.reason: WebFetch returned HTTP 403 Forbidden for both https://www.faa.gov/uas/advanced_operations/nepa_and_drones and the draft EA PDF on 2026-09-24. No claim was dropped for this reason. Every claim was verified against the showrunner's same-day curl copies instead, and each claim's verification field says so.
